aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is in full summer mode today with water at 86°F and calm east winds under 5 mph — ideal early-morning conditions for topwater on grass flats before the heat drives fish to deeper, shadier structure. Guides have been finding solid speckled trout and redfish numbers bay-wide, with bull reds and larger trout the standout catches in recent weeks; live bait has been the top producer, with artificials a workable secondary option. Plan to be on the water at first light and watch the western sky after 1 PM, when today's 23% storm chance kicks in — have a bailout spot picked before you launch.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides and concentrates trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around the pilings year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on an incoming tide, while the open-water exposure here means it's typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when wind or chop picks up.
bridge.todaysCall: With east winds at 0–5 mph today, the bridge should be calm and fishable — light current through the pilings will make the lee side productive as the tide ebbs toward the 1:42 PM low. Work the pilings early with topwater or suspending plugs for trout, then transition to live or cut bait near bottom for black drum and sheepshead as the sun climbs. The waning crescent moon is producing a spring-tide tidal push, which should amplify current through the funnel and concentrate bait nicely. Just keep the afternoon storm window in mind — open water here gives you no shelter if cells build after 1 PM, so plan to wrap up or relocate well before then.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder working the mouth; the oyster bars at the creek entrance are the prime focal point. Tree cover keeps interior temperatures a few degrees cooler than the open bay and provides reliable shelter from wind and building weather.
alaqua.todaysCall: The tree canopy and protected character make Alaqua a smart call on a hot August morning — head straight to the oyster bars at the mouth as the tide drops toward the 1:42 PM low and bait gets funneled out. The spring-tide push from the waning crescent should generate a little extra current off those bars, which is exactly what redfish and trout need to set up an ambush. Slightly stained water today actually favors a noisy or dark topwater early, then switch to live bait or a slow-sinking soft plastic once the sun is up. If afternoon storms develop after 1 PM, the interior of the bayou gives you a natural bailout — shorter run back to shelter than most spots on this list.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees lighter pressure than neighboring Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to produce less-wary fish — a genuine advantage on busy summer weekends. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer.
basin.todaysCall: Lower pressure makes Basin worth the trip on a Saturday when other bayous get crowded — the interior grass flats could hold reds willing to eat in the early window before heat drives them off the flat. Fish the mouth on the ebbing tide this morning while current is still moving, then push inside to look for reds on the flats if clarity allows — slightly stained water will limit sight-fishing range, so polarized lenses and patience matter more than usual. Live shrimp or a weedless gold spoon are good choices given the stain. Basin is less sheltered than LaGrange when weather builds, so keep an eye on the western sky and plan to exit before the post-1 PM storm window opens.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer in this area, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round; deep interior holes also concentrate black drum and sheepshead. It's the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the default choice when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange should be firing on all cylinders today — hit the oyster bars at the mouth right at first light with topwater or a popping cork over live shrimp while the spring-tide ebb is still generating current. Recent bay-wide reports flag speckled trout and redfish as the dominant inshore bite, and LaGrange's oyster structure is exactly the habitat that supports those patterns through the summer heat. As the morning progresses and the tide drops toward the 1:42 PM low, probe the deeper interior holes for black drum and sheepshead with cut crab or fiddler crabs on bottom. The most protected water on this side of the bay also means you can stay longer if afternoon storms threaten — but still monitor conditions and don't push your luck past 1 PM.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a short tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, and tidal flow funnels baitfish up into the bends and grass edges on incoming tides, concentrating redfish and trout. The creek mouth is a reliable flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water where bass join small reds.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile is one of the safest choices on today's dashboard given the afternoon storm risk — it's a short, protected fishery with a quick run back to the marina if weather builds after 1 PM. Focus on the creek mouth for flounder this morning, then work the bends and grass edges as the tide ebbs toward the 1:42 PM low and bait concentrates in the tighter water. Slightly stained water today is no obstacle here; in fact, reds and trout in a tidal creek tend to rely more on lateral-line feel than sight, so a rattle trap or noisy soft plastic can be productive alongside live bait. Keep an eye on tide timing — the transition around low at 1:42 PM often resets the bite, and a quick moving tide off the waning crescent spring push could bring a second flurry of activity.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on the bay, with trout stacking on grass in two to four feet of water on summer mornings. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides, and despite regular guide pressure, the spot produces reliably season after season.
hogtown.todaysCall: A Santa Rosa Beach-area guide reported solid speckled trout numbers and a notable bull redfish encounter in this part of the bay in late July — Hogtown fits squarely in that productive zone. Be on the grass flats early; summer mornings before 9 AM are peak time here before fish push off to deeper structure as the heat builds. Work a topwater plug or a popping cork with live shrimp across the two-to-four-foot grass zone, and check the mouth for mackerel on any moving current, especially as the tide runs down toward the 1:42 PM low. Factor in the longer run from the 331 Bridge area — leave early enough to fish the prime morning window, and build in departure time well before the post-1 PM storm window given the open-water exposure.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport, and its direct connection to that top-producing system means LaGrange's oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, less-pressured water. Documented fishing history for Mallet itself is limited, but its small, interior character makes it a natural calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: With LaGrange's recent trout and redfish bite running strong, Mallet is worth exploring as a low-pressure extension of that same system — fish the connection point between the two first, then probe any oyster or grass structure you find inside. Light east winds today mean even the more exposed spots are calm, but Mallet's interior position still makes it a sensible afternoon fallback if storms begin to develop after 1 PM. Stained water won't hurt you here; use a noisy or scented presentation — live shrimp under a popping cork or a paddle-tail soft plastic — to help fish locate the bait. Expectations should be measured given the limited documentation, but the habitat connection to LaGrange makes it a reasonable bonus stop if you're already working that bayou system.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination that's best planned as a dedicated trip. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, and sees less pressure simply because of the distance involved; Hewett and Buck Bayous immediately to the east are realistically fishable in the same outing.
mack.todaysCall: If you're committed to the run west today, the light east winds and calm morning conditions make this one of the better days to make that trip — seas on the main bay should stay flat until early afternoon. Target the oyster bars and marsh-grass edges early for trout and reds, then probe interior holes as the tide drops toward the 1:42 PM low. The spring-tide ebb from the waning crescent moon should produce a defined current push at the mouth — position there with live shrimp or a jig during the strongest part of that run. The 23% storm chance after 1 PM is the main concern on a long-run spot like this; plan your departure from the 30-A side to put you safely back at the ramp well before afternoon convection has a chance to build.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, sharing the same protected-bayou habitat — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth, deeper interior holes further in. Light fishing pressure due to its distance from the main ramps makes it an attractive pairing with Mack and Buck Bayou on the same trip.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes best as part of a dedicated western-bay run, and today's calm east winds make the transit manageable — plan to arrive well before 9 AM to catch the prime morning bite on the grass and oyster edges. Work the mouth structure on the ebbing tide and look for trout and reds setting up on current seams as the spring-tide push runs water out ahead of the 1:42 PM low. Slightly stained water may limit visual presentations, so lean on live bait or a scented paddle-tail that fish can track without seeing clearly. As with Mack and Buck, the afternoon storm window is your main logistical constraint — build your turnaround time aggressively to account for the long run back to the east.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track Mack and Hewett — marsh grass, some oyster structure, a modest interior — but there's limited basis to speak with confidence about it, and it's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck makes the most sense as a quick exploratory stop after you've worked Mack and Hewett — spend 20 to 30 minutes probing the mouth structure and any visible grass or oyster edges before moving on. Live shrimp or a small jig are versatile enough to cover the likely redfish, trout, and flounder mix without overthinking the presentation. The limited documentation here means you're fishing on habitat inference rather than a proven track record, so don't anchor your whole day to this spot. Given the afternoon storm risk and the long run back from the 30-A side, treat Buck as an early-morning bonus stop and prioritize getting underway for the return trip well before 1 PM.
